subject: ela
intro: A strong presentation states a clear claim, supports it in a logical order with pertinent facts and details, and is delivered with good eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation. In each item below, read the embedded outline, transcript, or description, then arrange, evaluate, or revise the presentation. Write your answer and explain your reasoning.

items.prompt: A student is planning a presentation and has these four points in scrambled order: (1) 'Last winter, two students slipped on the icy front steps.' (2) 'Our school should add a covered walkway to the main entrance.' (3) 'A covered walkway would keep the steps dry and safe in bad weather.' (4) 'The walkway could be built over the summer break.' Put the four points in the most logical order for presenting a claim and its findings, and explain why.
items.answer: Order: 2, 1, 3, 4. The speaker states the claim first, then shows the problem, then explains how the idea solves it, then gives the plan.

steps: Find the claim: point 2 states the main position, so it should come first.
Show the problem next: point 1 gives the reason the walkway is needed (students slipped), so it follows the claim.
Explain the solution: point 3 connects the walkway to keeping the steps safe, building on the problem.
End with the plan: point 4 tells when it could be built, which is the natural last step.
The logical order is 2, 1, 3, 4: claim, problem, solution, plan.

items.prompt: Read this part of a presentation: 'Our town should build a new public library. The current library has only ten computers, and on most afternoons every one of them is in use with students waiting in line.' One sentence is the claim and one provides the supporting findings. Identify which is which and explain how you can tell.
items.answer: The first sentence ('Our town should build a new public library') is the claim. The second sentence is the supporting finding because it gives a specific fact (only ten computers, all in use with students waiting) that backs up the claim.

steps: A claim states a position the speaker wants the audience to accept.
The first sentence argues that the town should build a new library, which is a position, so it is the claim.
The second sentence reports specific facts: ten computers and students waiting in line.
Facts and details that prove a point are the supporting findings, not the claim itself.
So the first sentence is the claim and the second provides the supporting findings.

items.prompt: A speaker is presenting the claim 'Our school should offer a recycling club.' Read the four supporting points: (1) 'A recycling club at a nearby school cut paper waste by a third in one year.' (2) 'Students could meet once a week after school.' (3) 'My older brother once won a science fair with a project about plastic.' (4) 'A teacher has already offered to be the club advisor.' Which point is not pertinent to the claim and should be cut? Explain why the other three should stay.
items.answer: Point 3 should be cut. A story about a brother winning a science fair does not support the claim that the school should offer a recycling club. Points 1, 2, and 4 stay because they show the club would work, how it could run, and that an advisor is ready.

steps: The claim is that the school should offer a recycling club.
Point 1 shows a similar club succeeded, which supports the claim.
Point 2 explains how the club could meet, a practical detail that supports it.
Point 4 shows an advisor is available, removing an obstacle to the claim.
Point 3 is about a brother's science fair project and does not support starting a club, so it is off topic and should be cut.

items.prompt: Read this description of a presentation: 'Marcus organized his report clearly, moving from his claim to his evidence to his plan. But he spoke so quietly that students in the back row could not hear him, and he kept his eyes on his note cards the whole time.' Which two delivery features most need improvement, and what specific change should Marcus make for each?
items.answer: Volume and eye contact. Marcus should speak louder so the back row can hear him, and he should look up at the audience instead of reading his note cards the whole time.

steps: The description praises his organization, so the problem is delivery, not content.
Students in the back could not hear him, which is a volume problem.
He kept his eyes on his note cards the whole time, which is an eye contact problem.
To fix volume, he should speak louder so everyone can hear.
To fix eye contact, he should look up at the audience while presenting.

items.prompt: A student claims 'The cafeteria should offer a vegetarian main dish every day.' Which of these supporting details is the most pertinent and specific? (A) 'Vegetables are healthy.' (B) 'A survey of students found that one in four would choose a vegetarian main dish if one were offered.' (C) 'I had a great veggie burger at a restaurant last weekend.' (D) 'Lunch is the best part of the day.' Choose the best detail and explain why the others are weaker.
items.answer: B is the best supporting detail. It is a specific, sourced fact (a survey showing one in four students would choose the option) that directly supports offering a vegetarian dish daily. A is too vague, C is a personal experience that is off topic, and D is an unrelated opinion.

steps: Strong support is relevant, specific, and based on facts, not opinion.
B gives survey data showing real demand for the dish, which directly supports the claim.
A says 'vegetables are healthy,' which is vague and does not address daily cafeteria offerings.
C is a personal story about a restaurant, not about the school cafeteria.
D is an unrelated opinion about lunch, so B is the single best choice.

items.prompt: A student wants to present these five points in the most logical order: (1) 'Here is a simple plan to plant a class garden in the courtyard.' (2) 'Our class should start a school garden.' (3) 'A class that started a garden last year grew enough vegetables to share with families.' (4) 'Right now the courtyard is an empty, unused space.' (5) 'A garden would give us fresh food and a place to learn outdoors.' Arrange the points in the best order and explain your reasoning.
items.answer: Order: 2, 4, 5, 3, 1. The speaker states the claim, shows the unused space, explains the benefits, gives evidence it has worked elsewhere, and ends with the plan.

steps: Point 2 is the claim that the class should start a garden, so it comes first.
Point 4 shows the empty courtyard, the current situation the garden would improve.
Point 5 explains the benefits of a garden, building the case.
Point 3 gives evidence that another class succeeded, strengthening the case.
Point 1 ends with the concrete plan, so the order is 2, 4, 5, 3, 1.

items.prompt: Read this short transcript: 'Schools should start a peer tutoring program. At a school across town, students who got peer tutoring raised their math grades. Also, the gym there has a really nice new floor.' One sentence weakens the presentation because it is off topic. Identify that sentence and explain why it does not belong.
items.answer: The sentence 'Also, the gym there has a really nice new floor' weakens the presentation. The claim is about a peer tutoring program, and a new gym floor has nothing to do with tutoring, so it is an irrelevant detail that should be cut.

steps: The claim is that schools should start a peer tutoring program.
The sentence about raised math grades is relevant evidence that tutoring helps.
The sentence about the gym floor mentions the same school but a different topic.
A detail that shares a setting but not the topic does not support the claim.
So the gym floor sentence is off topic and should be removed.

items.prompt: Two students gave presentations on the claim 'Our class should adopt a class pet.' Sara stated her claim, gave three relevant facts in a clear order, but mumbled so quietly that half the room could not follow her. Devon spoke loudly and clearly with good eye contact, but jumped between unrelated points and never clearly stated his claim. Which student's presentation needs the bigger fix in content versus delivery, and what should each one work on?
items.answer: Sara needs to fix delivery: she should speak louder and more clearly so everyone can hear her. Devon needs to fix content and organization: he should state his claim clearly and put his points in a logical order. Sara's content is strong but her delivery is weak, while Devon's delivery is strong but his content is weak.

steps: Judge both content and delivery, not just one.
Sara had clear, well ordered content, so her problem is delivery: volume and clear pronunciation.
Sara should speak louder and pronounce words clearly so the whole room can follow.
Devon spoke well but had no clear claim and jumped between points, so his problem is content and organization.
Devon should state his claim clearly and arrange his points in a logical order.

items.prompt: Read this part of a presentation: 'Our school should add a homework help session after school. Test scores went up by twelve points at a school that added one.' A classmate says the second sentence is the claim. Is the classmate correct? Identify the real claim and the supporting finding, and explain the difference.
items.answer: The classmate is incorrect. The first sentence ('Our school should add a homework help session after school') is the claim. The second sentence, about test scores rising by twelve points, is a supporting finding. A claim states a position, while the statistic is a specific fact used to back it up.

steps: A claim is the position the speaker is arguing for.
The first sentence argues the school should add a homework help session, so it is the claim.
The second sentence reports a specific number, twelve points, which is a fact.
A statistic is a supporting detail, not the main position, even though it sounds confident.
So the first sentence is the claim and the second is the supporting finding.

items.prompt: A student claims 'Our class should take a field trip to the science museum.' Read the four supporting points the student plans to use: (1) 'The museum has a hands-on exhibit that matches our unit on energy.' (2) 'Tickets are discounted for school groups, so the trip would be affordable.' (3) 'The bus ride takes about thirty minutes.' (4) 'My family went to a water park last summer.' Which point should be cut as irrelevant, and which point is the strongest support for the claim? Explain both choices.
items.answer: Point 4 should be cut because a family trip to a water park has nothing to do with a class trip to the science museum. Point 1 is the strongest support because it shows the museum directly connects to what the class is studying.

steps: The claim is that the class should visit the science museum.
Point 4 is about a water park, an unrelated topic, so it is off topic and should be cut.
Point 1 links the museum's exhibit to the class unit on energy, giving a strong learning reason.
Points 2 and 3 are relevant but weaker: cost and travel time are practical, not the main reason.
So cut point 4 and use point 1 as the strongest support.

items.prompt: Read this description: 'During his talk on school recycling, Jordan spoke at a good volume, but he rushed his words so fast that the audience could not catch many of them, and he stared at the back wall instead of at the listeners.' Which two delivery features need improvement, and what should Jordan do for each? Be careful to name the correct features.
items.answer: Clear pronunciation and eye contact need improvement. Jordan should slow down and speak clearly so the audience can catch his words, and he should look at the listeners instead of the back wall. His volume was already good, so that does not need fixing.

steps: The description says his volume was good, so volume is not the problem.
He rushed his words so they could not be understood, which is a clear pronunciation problem.
He stared at the back wall instead of the listeners, which is an eye contact problem.
To fix pronunciation, he should slow down and speak each word clearly.
To fix eye contact, he should look at the audience rather than the wall.

items.prompt: A student is presenting the claim 'Students should be allowed to bring water bottles to class.' Which choice is the most pertinent and specific supporting detail? (A) 'Water is important.' (B) 'I get thirsty sometimes.' (C) 'A school nurse reported that students who stay hydrated have fewer afternoon headaches and stay more focused.' (D) 'My favorite water bottle is blue.' Choose the best detail and explain why the other three are weak.
items.answer: C is the best supporting detail. It is a specific, sourced fact (a nurse's report linking hydration to fewer headaches and better focus) that supports allowing water bottles in class. A is too vague, B is a personal feeling, and D is an unrelated detail about a bottle's color.

steps: Strong support is specific, relevant, and based on facts rather than opinion.
C cites a school nurse and gives concrete benefits, directly supporting the claim.
A says 'water is important,' which is vague and does not connect to classroom rules.
B is a personal feeling, and D is about a bottle's color, both off topic.
So C is the single best supporting detail.

items.prompt: A student plans to present these points in scrambled order: (1) 'A team that practiced mindfulness reported feeling calmer before games.' (2) 'Our school should add a short mindfulness break before tests.' (3) 'Many students say they feel very nervous right before a test.' (4) 'The break could be just five minutes of quiet breathing.' Put the points in the most logical order, and explain why starting with point 1 would be a mistake.
items.answer: Order: 2, 3, 1, 4. Starting with point 1 would be a mistake because the audience would hear evidence before they know the claim or the problem it addresses, so the evidence would not make sense yet. The logical order states the claim, shows the problem, gives evidence it works, then explains the plan.

steps: Point 2 states the claim, so it should come first.
Point 3 shows the problem of test nervousness, which the break would address.
Point 1 gives evidence that mindfulness helped another group, supporting the idea.
Point 4 explains the simple plan, so it comes last.
Beginning with point 1 puts evidence before the claim and problem, so listeners would not yet know what it supports.

items.prompt: Read this transcript: 'Our class should write thank-you letters to local firefighters. Last month the fire station helped put out a kitchen fire two blocks from school. Firefighters often work long, hard shifts. Also, my uncle owns a really fast red car.' Identify the one sentence that is off topic, then put the remaining sentences in the most logical order for the presentation.
items.answer: The off-topic sentence is 'Also, my uncle owns a really fast red car,' which has nothing to do with thanking firefighters and should be cut. A logical order for the rest is: claim ('Our class should write thank-you letters to local firefighters'), then the reason ('Firefighters often work long, hard shifts'), then the local example ('Last month the fire station helped put out a kitchen fire two blocks from school').

steps: The claim is that the class should write thank-you letters to firefighters.
The sentence about an uncle's red car shares no topic with firefighters, so it is off topic and is cut.
State the claim first so the audience knows the position.
Give the general reason next: firefighters work long, hard shifts.
End with the specific local example of the kitchen fire to make the reason concrete.

items.prompt: A student gave this presentation: 'Our school should plant more trees on the playground. The shade would keep students cooler on hot days. A study found that shaded playgrounds stay up to ten degrees cooler. Trees are also pretty to look at.' The student spoke clearly but read every word from a paper and never looked up. Name one content improvement and one delivery improvement that would most strengthen this presentation, and explain each choice.
items.answer: Content improvement: cut or strengthen 'Trees are also pretty to look at,' which is a weak opinion compared with the cooling facts; the speaker could replace it with another solid fact or simply remove it to keep the findings focused. Delivery improvement: the speaker should look up at the audience instead of reading every word from the paper, improving eye contact.

steps: Check the content: the claim is supported by strong facts about shade and cooler temperatures.
The line 'Trees are also pretty to look at' is a weak opinion that adds little, so cutting or replacing it focuses the findings.
Check the delivery: the speaker spoke clearly, so pronunciation and volume are fine.
The speaker read every word and never looked up, which is an eye contact problem.
So the best fixes are removing the weak opinion and looking up at the audience for eye contact.
